# Detect candidate loci under selection

In 'RISG_dDocent_working' directory, make new directory for outlier detection and link vcf files and popmap file.
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working
mkdir RISG_Outlier_Detection_working
cd RISG_Outlier_Detection_working

cp ../RISG_SNP_Filtering_working/SNP.TRSdp5g75mafPM9g9maf1.2A.nDNA.FIL.recode.vcf .
cp ../RISG_SNP_Filtering_working/popmap .
```

I am going to combine three methods to detect outliers:
- PCAdapt: assumption-light; detects outliers associated with genetic structure, but may over-identify candidates
- OutFLANK: more stringent; identifies outliers based on Fst differentiation
- LFMM: best suited for genotype–environment associations, while accounting for population structure.
(BayeScan not used as old Fst-based method; generally less powerful than other approaches)

## 1. PCAdapt

Assumes that genetic variants (SNPs) that are excessively correlated with population structure are outliers, making them strong candidates for being under natural selection. It first captures the overarching population structure by performing PCA on centered and scaled genotype data. It infers structure directly from the genetic data, doesn't required to group individuals into explicit populations beforehand.

Load in R:
```{r}
# Install and load pcadapt
#install.packages("pcadapt")
library(pcadapt)
```

```{r}
# Convert VCF file to pcadapt format
vcf2pcadapt("SNP.TRSdp5g75mafPM9g9maf1.2A.nDNA.FIL.recode.vcf", output = "SNP.pcadapt", allele.sep = c("/", "|"))
filename <- read.pcadapt("SNP.pcadapt", type = "pcadapt")
```

```{r}
# Choosing the number K of Principal Components
# We start off with a large number of PCs
RISGpops <- pcadapt(input = filename, K = 20)
```

```{r}
# Plot the likelihoods using a scree plot
plot(RISGpops, option = "screeplot")
```
Cattell’s rule indicates K = 6.

```{r}
# Create population designations
poplist.names <- c(rep("BAR", 10), rep("BIS", 10), rep("CS", 20), rep("GB", 10), rep("HA", 20),
                   rep("HC", 20), rep("HI", 20), rep("HO", 20), rep("KIC", 10), rep("MCD", 9),
                   rep("M", 20), rep("MW", 20), rep("NB", 20), rep("PVD", 10), rep("SR", 20))
```

```{r}
# Create estuary designations
estuarylist.names <- ifelse(poplist.names %in% c("BAR", "BIS", "GB", "KIC", "MCD", "PVD"), "NB",
                            ifelse(poplist.names %in% c("CS", "HC", "M", "NB", "SR"), "DB",
                                   ifelse(poplist.names %in% c("HA", "HI", "HO", "MW"), "CB",
                                          NA)))
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

pca.pop <- as.data.frame(RISGpops$score)
pca.pop$Populations <- poplist.names

# Define colors and shapes for each population
pop_fills <- c("BIS"="#004700", "MCD"="#006b00", "GB"="#008f00", "KIC"="#19ba19", "BAR"="#7fd97f","PVD"="#ccefcc",
                "CS"="#00007f", "NB"="#0000bf", "SR"="#0000ff", "M"="#5959ff", "HC"="#b2b2ff",
                "HI"="#990000", "HO"="#d90000", "HA"="#ff3232", "MW"="#ff7373")
pop_colors <- c("BIS"="white", "MCD"="white", "GB"="white", "KIC"="white", "BAR"="white","PVD"="white",
                "CS"="white", "NB"="white", "SR"="white", "M"="white", "HC"="white",
                "HI"="white", "HO"="white", "HA"="white", "MW"="white")
pop_shapes <- c("BIS"=21, "MCD"=21, "GB"=21, "KIC"=21, "BAR"=21,"PVD"=21,
                "CS"=21, "NB"=21, "SR"=21, "M"=21, "HC"=21,
                "HI"=21, "HO"=21, "HA"=21, "MW"=21)

# Make score plot
ggplot(pca.pop, aes(x = V1, y = V2, color = Populations, fill = Populations, shape = Populations)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pop_fills) +
  scale_color_manual(values = pop_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = pop_shapes) +
  theme(panel.background = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color="black", fill=NA, linewidth=0.5),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(color="gray90", linewidth=0.15),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(0.2, colour = "black"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(color="black", size=9),
        axis.text.y = element_text(color="black", size=9),
        axis.ticks = element_line(color = "black"),
        axis.title.x = element_text(color="black", size=9),
        axis.title.y = element_text(color="black", size=9),
        legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "PC1", y = "PC2")
```

We clearly see 3 clusters per bay, this is characteristic of inversions -> we need to look into the 3 genotypes of these inversions for each bay.

```{r}
# Score Plot
# Plot the first two PCs
plot(RISGpops, option = "scores", pop = poplist.names)
```

```{r}
# PCA plot with PC3 and 4
plot(RISGpops, option = "scores", i = 3, j = 4, pop = estuarylist.names)
```

Evaluating LD in dataset -> looking to see if loadings are clustered in certain genomic regions (following https://bcm-uga.github.io/pcadapt/articles/pcadapt.html#f--linkage-disequilibrium-ld-thinning)

Linkage disequilibrium (LD) = non-random association of alleles at two or more different loci in a population, meaning certain combinations of alleles are inherited together more or less often than expected by chance.
-> can affect ascertainment of population structure, dense SNP data should account for LD in their genome scans.

Inversion -> unusually strong/extended LD across a large genomic region = regions of low recombination.
Clues of inversion: PCA shows 3 discrete clusters and the SNPs driving the separation are concentrated on one chromosome.

```{r}
# To evaluate if LD might be an issue for dataset, display the loadings (contributions of each SNP to the PC) and evaluate if the loadings are clustered in a single or several genomic regions.
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (i in 1:4)
  plot(RISGpops$loadings[, i], pch = 19, cex = .3, ylab = paste0("Loadings PC", i))
```
We see that PC2 and PC3 are determined by two genomic regions of strong LD, also maybe one region in PC1.
We should therefore thin SNPs in order to compute the PCS = apply LD thinning.
I'm going to use the default values for window size and r2 threshold for pcadapt (size = 200, thr = 0.1 -> good general starting point and conservative choice for thr).
However I still see these two strong LD regions in PC2, and now also in PC4 -> I will modify parameters of SNP thinning.
- size = window size -> the number of SNPs considered around each SNP, not a physical distance in bp (size = 500 more aggressive genomic thinning if strong/long-range LD).
- thr = r² threshold -> SNPs with LD above this threshold are thinned so that highly correlated markers don't disproportionately influence PCA (thr = 0.05 very stringent if strong LD or very dense data).

It's better to increase the size value until the clusters disappear from PC loadings (these inversion regions are large), because a thr = 0.1 is already very low.

```{r}
# Performing SNP thinning in order to compute PCs
res <- pcadapt(filename, K = 20, LD.clumping = list(size = 5000, thr = 0.05))
plot(res, option = "screeplot")
```

After SNP thinning, we choose K = 4.
Size = 5000 -> we still see the cluster regions in PC2 loadings.
Size = 7500 -> we still see the cluster regions in PC2 loadings.
Size = 10000 -> we still see the cluster regions in PC2 loadings (still smaller than the inversion region).
Size = 20000 -> we still see the cluster regions in PC2 loadings.
Size = 50000 -> we still see the cluster regions in PC2 loadings.
Size = 100000 -> we still see the cluster regions in PC2 loadings.

```{r}
res <- pcadapt(filename, K = 4, LD.clumping = list(size = 5000, thr = 0.1))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (i in 1:4)
  plot(res$loadings[, i], pch = 19, cex = .3, ylab = paste0("Loadings PC", i))
```

```{r}
res <- pcadapt(filename, K = 4, LD.clumping = list(size = 5000, thr = 0.05))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (i in 1:4)
  plot(res$loadings[, i], pch = 19, cex = .3, ylab = paste0("Loadings PC", i))
```

```{r}
res <- pcadapt(filename, K = 4, LD.clumping = list(size = 10000, thr = 0.05))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (i in 1:4)
  plot(res$loadings[, i], pch = 19, cex = .3, ylab = paste0("Loadings PC", i))
```

```{r}
plot(res, option = "manhattan")
# The cluster/inversion regions will be still visible on the Manhattan plot, it's normal. We want the clusters to disappear from the background on the PC loadings though.
```

```{r}
res$singular.values
```

### Save outliers

Choosing a cutoff for outlier detection
We can be more strict here with alpha = 0.05 as PCAdapt has less assumptions and overpick outliers 
```{r}
library(qvalue) #transforms p-values into q-values

qval <- qvalue(res$pvalues)$qvalues
alpha <- 0.05 #expected false discovery rate lower than 5%

# Save outliers
pcadapt.outliers <- which(qval < alpha)
length(pcadapt.outliers)
```

Before LD-thinning: 7522 outliers

After LD-thinning:
Size 5000 / thr 0.1 =  6262 outliers
Size 10000 / thr 0.1 = 5782
Size 20000 / thr 0.1 = 5830
Size 5000 / thr 0.05 = 4407 -> good one, having the smallest size and higher thr to get rid of the clusters in PC loadings. 
Size 10000 / thr 0.05 = 4045
Size 20000 / thr 0.05 = 4062

```{r}
# Save outliers to .txt file 
invisible(lapply(pcadapt.outliers, write, "outliers_pcadapt_thinned.txt", append=TRUE))
```

Taking the SNP indices and applying chromosome and position info:
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/RISG_Outlier_Detection_working

cat  outliers_pcadapt_thinned.txt | parallel "grep -w ^{} loci1.plus.index" | cut -f2,3> outliers_pcadapt_thinned.loci.txt

```

## 2. OutFLANK

https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/whitlock/OutFLANK/blob/master/inst/doc/OutFLANKAnalysis.html

```{r}
# Load all necessary packages
library(OutFLANK)  # outflank package
library(vcfR)
library(bigsnpr)   # package for Linkage Disequilibrium pruning
```

```{r}
# Convert VCF to OutFLANK format
vcf_OutFLANK <- read.vcfR("SNP.TRSdp5g75mafPM9g9maf1.2A.nDNA.FIL.recode.vcf")
```
File attributes:
  meta lines: 96
  header_line: 97
  variant count: 197634
  column count: 248

```{r}
geno <- extract.gt(vcf_OutFLANK) # Character matrix containing the genotypes
position <- getPOS(vcf_OutFLANK) # Positions in bp
chromosome <- getCHROM(vcf_OutFLANK) # Chromosome information

G <- matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(geno), ncol = ncol(geno))

G[geno %in% c("0/0", "0|0")] <- 0
G[geno  %in% c("0/1", "1/0", "1|0", "0|1")] <- 1
G[geno %in% c("1/1", "1|1")] <- 2

# NA should be replaced with “9” to work with the functions in the OutFLANK package
G[is.na(G)] <- 9

head(G[,1:10])
```
```{r}
# Convert pop designations to a vector
pop <- as.vector(poplist.names)
pop
```

```{r}
# Calculate FST
FST_OutFLANK <- MakeDiploidFSTMat(t(G), locusNames = paste0(chromosome,"_", position), popNames = pop)
head(FST_OutFLANK) # the output will be a table showing Fst statistics for each locus
```

```{r}
# Plot heterozygosity vs FST
plot(FST_OutFLANK$He, FST_OutFLANK$FST)
```
FST = 0 -> allele frequencies are identical in all populations (no differentiation).
FST = 1 -> populations are fixed for different alleles (complete differentiation).
If high FST SNP, it means one population has a very different allele frequency than another, a signal of local adaptation or drift.

The bulk of SNPs form a "wedge" shape = neutral expectation. OutFLANK fits a chi-squared distribution to the right side (high He SNPs) to model neutral FST, then identifies outliers above the distribution.

```{r}
# Plot FST vs FSTNoCorr
plot(FST_OutFLANK$FST, FST_OutFLANK$FSTNoCorr)
abline(0,1)
```
STNoCorr = Fst without sample size correction.
The line sits just above the diagonal (FSTNoCorr > FST), which is expected -> the uncorrected value is always a bit inflated. The offset is small and uniform, indicating your sampling is well-balanced.

### We need to give OutFLANK a set of quasi-independent SNPs to estimate the neutral FST distribution.

```{r}
# Load additional packages
library("dplyr")
library("stringr")
```

```{r}
# Chromosomes need to be of class integer for this to work.
# Visualizing chromosomes
chrom_unique <- unique(chromosome)
print(chrom_unique)
```

```{r}
# Removing "NC_" from the chromosome name so it can be converted to an integer
chrom_new <- chromosome%>%str_replace("NC_","")

# Converting the character string into an integer
chrom1 <- as.integer(chrom_new)
```

```{r}
# Chromosome and position need to be sorted for imputation to work.
chrom_sort <- sort(chrom1)
pos_sort <- sort(position)
```

### Note: This filtering program does not allow for missing genotype values.

Using `snp_fastImputeSimple` to impute missing genotypes

```{r}
# Converting the genotype matrix to class FBM.code256
G1 <- add_code256(big_copy(t(G),type="raw"),code=bigsnpr:::CODE_012)

# Imputing missing genotypes
G_missSimple <- snp_fastImputeSimple(G1,method = "mode")
```

```{r}
newpc <- snp_autoSVD(G_missSimple, infos.chr = chrom_sort,infos.pos = pos_sort)
# LD pruning = removes SNPs in high linkage disequilibrium with each other. The pruning is important for OutFLANK because correlated SNPs violate the assumption of independence.
which_pruned <- attr(newpc, which="subset") # Indexes of remaining SNPS after pruning
length(which_pruned)
```

### Run the OutFLANK() function to estimate the parameters on the neutral FST distribution.

```{r}
out_trim <- OutFLANK(FST_OutFLANK[which_pruned,], NumberOfSamples = 15, qthreshold = 0.05, Hmin = 0.1)
str(out_trim)
# NumberOfSamples = number of populations
```

```{r}
# Check the fit and make sure it looks good, especially in the right tail:
OutFLANKResultsPlotter(out_trim, withOutliers = TRUE, NoCorr = TRUE, Hmin = 0.1, binwidth = 0.001, Zoom = FALSE, RightZoomFraction = 0.05, titletext = NULL)
```
```{r}
# To inspect closely the right tail, which is the critical part:
OutFLANKResultsPlotter(out_trim, withOutliers = TRUE, NoCorr = TRUE, Hmin = 0.1, binwidth = 0.005, Zoom = TRUE, RightZoomFraction = 0.05)
```
This plot shows a poor fit, the blue curve and orange histogram are misaligned.
The model is shifted to the left relative to your data -> it underestimates the typical neutral Fst.
The right tail of the blue curve falls below the orange bars at moderate Fst values (0.1–0.2), meaning OutFLANK will call too many false positives -> SNPs that are just neutrally differentiated will be flagged as outliers.

```{r}
# Check the p-value histogram
hist(out_trim$results$pvaluesRightTail)
```

Under a well-fitted model, neutral SNPs should have uniformly distributed p-values between 0 and 1, with a spike at 0 from true outliers (adaptive SNPs).
My histogram is roughly uniform across 0–1 with a modest spike at 0 and another bump at 1. This is not ideal!
The bump at p ≈ 1 is a red flag -> it means many SNPs have extremely high p-values, suggesting the neutral distribution is still shifted too far right relative to the data (model overestimates neutral FST for many SNPs).

```{r}
# Using estimated neutral mean FST and df to calculate P-values for all loci
P1 <- pOutlierFinderChiSqNoCorr(FST_OutFLANK, Fstbar = out_trim$FSTNoCorrbar, dfInferred = out_trim$dfInferred, qthreshold = 0.05, Hmin=0.1)
```

```{r}
# Identify outliers SNPs
my_out <- P1$OutlierFlag==TRUE
plot(P1$He, P1$FST, pch=19, col=rgb(0,0,0,0.1))
points(P1$He[my_out], P1$FST[my_out], col="blue")
```

```{r}
P1[which(P1$OutlierFlag == TRUE),]

outliers_out <- P1[which(P1$OutlierFlag == TRUE),]
outliers_out
```

```{r}
# This is a bit complicated, but I'm saving the row names (snp numbers) as a column in the dataframe then extracting those values from the table to save to a .txt file 
out_outliers_list1_8pops <- outliers_out
out_outliers_list1_8pops$snps <- row.names(out_outliers_list1_8pops)
out_outliers_8pops <- out_outliers_list1_8pops$snps
```

```{r}
invisible(lapply(out_outliers_8pops, write, "outliers_outflank_8pops.txt", append=TRUE))
```
